options.content: A framework of members joined to form triangles
A solid steel beam with an I-shaped cross-section
options.rationale: A truss is an open framework.

options.content: A single cable in tension holding up a bridge
options.rationale: That is a tie or cable.

options.content: A curved arch of stone blocks in compression

explanation: A truss is a framework of members joined at their ends to form triangles.

stem: Why are trusses built from triangles?

options.content: A triangle cannot change shape unless a side changes length.
Triangles use the most material, so they are strongest.
Triangles look attractive and are easy to paint.
Triangles have no joints that could fail under load.

explanation: A pin-jointed triangle is rigid; a square can fold into a parallelogram without any member changing length.

options.content: A member in tension
A member carrying no force
The joint between two members
A member in compression

explanation: A strut is pushed: it is in compression.

options.content: A member in compression
A beam with an I-section
options.rationale: Not a definition of a tie.

options.content: A support at the end of a truss
A member in tension

explanation: A tie is pulled: it is in tension.

stem: A rope can be used as a strut in a framework.
explanation: A rope can only pull. It can act as a tie (tension) but folds up under compression, so it cannot be a strut.

stem: In a triangular roof truss, what is the main job of the horizontal tie beam at the bottom?

options.content: It holds up the roof sheets directly; it is in compression.
options.rationale: The rafters carry the roof sheets.

options.content: It stops the rafters pushing the walls out; it is in tension.
It is in compression and pushes the walls apart.
options.rationale: It pulls the rafter ends together.

options.content: It has no force in it and is only for hanging a ceiling.

explanation: The loaded rafters try to spread outwards at their feet; the tie beam pulls the feet together, so it is in tension.

stem: A learner replaces one member of a model truss with a piece of string. The frame still keeps its shape under load. What can she conclude?

options.content: That member was a strut (in compression).
options.rationale: String would go slack in compression.

options.content: That member was a tie (in tension).
That member carried no force at all.
options.rationale: It might carry tension; string shows it.

options.content: The truss no longer needs triangles.
options.rationale: The triangle shape is still there.

explanation: String can only pull. If it holds the frame, the member it replaced was pulled: a tie.
hints: What kind of force can a string carry?

stem: Why are struts usually made thicker than ties?

options.content: Struts carry less force.
Ties are stronger materials.
options.rationale: They may be the same material.

options.content: Struts are compressed and must not buckle.
Thicker members are always lighter for their strength.

explanation: Compressed members can buckle sideways if they are thin; members in tension cannot buckle, so ties can be thin, even cables.
hints: Which kind of member can buckle?

stem: Match each term with its meaning.

right.content: Dividing a frame into triangles to make it rigid
How much load a structure carries for its mass

explanation: Trusses use triangulation; their members are struts or ties, giving a high strength-to-mass ratio.

stem: An engineer must choose between a solid steel beam and a steel truss to span the roof of a new market hall.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Give three advantages of using a truss.

points.description: It is much lighter for the same strength (high strength-to-mass ratio)
It uses less material, so it is cheaper (economy)
It can span a wider gap; its members are mostly in pure tension or compression, the way materials are strongest

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which member of the truss would be most likely to need cross-bracing to stop it buckling?

options.content: A short tie
A long tie
A long strut
options.rationale: Correct: long compressed members can buckle.

options.content: The bolts at the joints

parts.explanation: Long members in compression are at risk of buckling, so they are braced.

explanation: Trusses give high strength for low mass and cost and span long gaps; long struts need bracing against buckling.
hints: Think about mass, cost and span.

stem: A rectangular wooden gate frame sags and twists into a parallelogram. What is the best fix?

options.content: Add another horizontal bar parallel to the first.
Paint the gate.
options.rationale: Paint does not stop it changing shape.

options.content: Add a diagonal brace to divide it into triangles.
Loosen the joints.

explanation: A diagonal turns the rectangle into two triangles, which cannot change shape.
